pieces.title: ShutterSense
pieces.summary: An experimental DSLR photography simulation built in Unity 6. It explores whether practical interaction with aperture, shutter, ISO, and light can make camera controls easier to understand.
body: Motivation: camera settings are usually taught as numbers before they are felt as consequences. ShutterSense asks whether a controllable scene can reverse that order.
The interaction model covers aperture, shutter speed, ISO, exposure, composition, and light. It is academic and experimental work, not a finished training product.
Educational effectiveness is not claimed. Demonstrations, research notes, and known limits will be added when recordings and write-ups exist.

pieces.title: What a simulation is allowed to teach
pieces.summary: A working note on the difference between a controllable model and a claim that someone learned from it.
body: A simulation can show a relationship: change the aperture and the depth of field changes. That is already useful. It is not the same as proving that a learner will transfer the idea to a real camera.
For this site, experimental work stays labeled experimental. A prototype does not become a product because the interface looks finished.
The useful next step is usually smaller than a paper: record the interaction, name the question, and write what the build cannot yet answer.

pieces.title: Two doors, one practice
pieces.summary: Why this site separates a research path from a collaboration path without splitting the person into two brands.
body: A researcher looking for method and a studio looking for an interface do not need the same first sentence. They can still arrive at the same photographs, films, and notes.
The homepage is organized as chapters with two explicit doors: Research & Academia, and Work & Collaborations. Visual work stays reachable from both.
